# Add wishlist

## Why
Customers lose track of products they like and leave without buying. A wishlist keeps what they liked within reach.

## What changes

### Add · wishlist/save-item
- A signed-in customer saves a product to their wishlist {#saves-item}
  e.g. Sanne saves "Rain jacket" -> it appears in her wishlist
- Saving the same product twice keeps one entry {#no-duplicates}
  e.g. Sanne saves "Rain jacket" again -> it still appears once
- A customer sees their saved products in the order they saved them {#lists-saved}
  e.g. Sanne saved a jacket, then a map -> the jacket is listed first

## Not doing
Sharing wishlists; price-drop alerts.

# Code Structure Guardrails

Use this skill as a preflight before writing code and as a checkpoint while editing. The goal is to keep code easy to move, test, review, and maintain without broad unrelated refactors.

## Preflight

Before writing code:

1. Read the project-local instructions, architecture notes, and existing patterns that govern the files you will touch.
2. Identify the correct layer before creating a file: page-only code, domain code, shared UI, shared utility, server/API layer, test helper, or config.
3. Define the smallest useful units before implementation: components, hooks, functions, schemas, constants, and tests.
4. Set a size budget. If a planned file or component looks like it will grow large, split it before writing it.
5. Name the responsibility of every new function or component in one short sentence. If the sentence needs "and", split it or extract a helper.

## File And Component Size

Keep source files small enough to scan.

- Treat 200 lines as a warning point for application code.
- Do not create or significantly expand hand-written source files beyond 300 lines unless there is a clear local convention or unavoidable framework constraint.
- Never use a 300-line, 500-line, or larger file as the easy path for mixed responsibilities.
- Exempt generated files, lockfiles, fixtures, schema dumps, and simple data/config tables unless the task is specifically to restructure them.

For React components:

- Split presentational sections from stateful orchestration when both are non-trivial.
- Move reusable business UI to the domain layer and pure reusable primitives to the shared UI layer, following the repository's conventions.
- Keep page files focused on routing, composition, and data boundaries.
- Extract repeated markup only when it has a clear name and stable responsibility.

## Function Design

Each function should do one thing.

- Prefer short functions with a single reason to change.
- Split functions that validate, transform, fetch, mutate, render, and format in the same body.
- Avoid boolean flags that make one function behave like several functions; prefer separate named functions or an options object with clear semantics.
- Keep side effects at the boundary and pure logic in small helpers where practical.
- Make extracted helpers local first. Promote them to shared modules only after reuse is real.

## Parameters And Data Shape

Keep call sites readable.

- Avoid long positional parameter lists.
- Use one object parameter when a function needs more than three inputs, when inputs are optional, or when several values travel together.
- Name object fields after domain concepts, not implementation details.
- Do not pass broad objects just to avoid choosing fields. Pass the narrow shape the function actually needs.

Example:

```ts
// Prefer this when inputs grow.
calculateInvoiceTotal({
  lineItems,
  discountCode,
  taxRate,
});
```

## Placement

Move code to the right folder when its responsibility is clear.

- Page-only view code belongs near the route.
- Reusable domain behavior belongs in the domain/module area.
- Reusable generic UI belongs in the shared UI area.
- Shared utilities must be framework-neutral unless the repository has a more specific convention.
- Tests should sit where the project expects them, close enough to make ownership obvious.

Follow local repository rules over these generic folder names.

## Existing Code

When touched code already violates these guardrails:

- Fix the issue if it is in the direct path of the requested change and can be done without changing behavior.
- Keep the fix surgical: split only the affected component/function/file section.
- Preserve public APIs unless the task explicitly allows changing them.
- If the problem is broad or outside the requested work, mention it instead of refactoring the whole area.

## Review Checklist

Before finalizing code, verify:

- New or changed code is in the correct project layer.
- No new large hand-written source file was created.
- Components have clear boundaries and no unrelated responsibilities.
- Functions do one thing and have readable call sites.
- Long parameter lists were replaced with typed object parameters where appropriate.
- Structural fixes stayed within the scope of touched code.
